characters: Obaa: a 13-year-old girl in a school uniform, with a laptop and a notebook.
Samir: a 13-year-old boy in a school uniform, who loves maps.
Mr Tweneboah: their geography teacher, in a short-sleeved shirt and glasses.
The Singapore River: a story picture of a dirty river that becomes a clean river with walkways, drawn as before and after.

narrationPlan.voice: Curious young voices for Obaa and Samir; clear, encouraging voice for Mr Tweneboah
narrationPlan.pace: Clear and hopeful, slower at the comparison (about 120 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Slow, murky tune becoming bright and flowing, like water clearing (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The Singapore River facts come from published histories. The pupils and teacher are invented.
The story compares places carefully and does not say that Ghana and Singapore are the same.
The claims about Ghana’s large drainage projects come from an opinion piece and a news report and are marked as claims to check.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check against named sources: master plan 1977; completion declared 2 September 1987; about 46,000 squatters resettled; about 5,000 hawkers moved to hawker centres; pig and duck farms moved; sewers and covered drains; float booms; about S$300 million excluding resettlement compensation.
Check that the story does not claim a public education campaign, which the source does not confirm.
Check the claims on the 2012 Odaw and Korle Lagoon project (about US$660 million) and the later flood project (about a third disbursed by mid-2025) with official sources before release.

teacherGuide.overview: A comparison story that shows a famous clean-up and asks what Ghana can learn from it. It teaches that a clean river takes a deadline, fair treatment, infrastructure, new habits and persistent leaders.
learningGoals: Describe how the Singapore River was cleaned.
Compare it with a local water body and say what is similar and different.
Explain why copying blindly is unwise.
beforeReading: Show before and after pictures of a river, or ask learners to draw one.
whileReading: At page 7, ask learners to list the four lessons and add one of their own.
afterReading: Draw a “before and after” picture of a local drain, stream or lagoon.
Write a short plan for a ten-year clean-up with a deadline.
discussion: Why was fairness to people who had to move so important?
Why might a clean river become dirty again?
reflection: What would you want your river to look like in ten years?

mathsExtension.task: From 1977 to 1987 is how many years?
About 46,000 people were resettled. If 4,000 were along the Singapore River, how many were around Kallang Basin?

support: Give learners a before-and-after table to fill in.
stretch: Compare the clean-up with another city’s river clean-up.

culturalNotes: The Singapore River facts come from published histories. The pupils and teacher are invented.
The story compares places carefully and does not say that Ghana and Singapore are the same.
The claims about Ghana’s large drainage projects come from an opinion piece and a news report and are marked as claims to check.
localiseThis: Use a local stream, drain or lagoon as the comparison; invite an assembly or environmental officer to speak.

whatWeKnow: The Singapore River was cleaned between 1977 and 1987 through planning, relocation, sewers and enforcement.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: How well the cost and results of Ghana’s own large drainage projects match what was promised.

factCheck.claim: The Singapore River clean-up ran about ten years (master plan 1977; declared complete 2 September 1987); about 46,000 squatters were resettled; about 5,000 hawkers moved to hawker centres; hundreds of pig and duck farms moved; about 800 lighters moved; sewers expanded; drains covered; float booms; cost about S$300 million excluding compensation; the source does not describe a public education campaign.
factCheck.explanation: From the National Library Board Singapore’s encyclopedia entry.
factCheck.reference: National Library Board Singapore, Infopedia, “Cleaning of the Singapore River” (eresources.nlb.gov.sg).

factCheck.claim: A project signed in 2012 to dredge the Odaw and restore the Korle Lagoon, at around US$660 million, did not deliver what was promised; a World Bank project (GARID) approved in 2019 had spent about 36% by mid-2025.
factCheck.explanation: From a JoyNews feature that argues the promised transformation did not come; figures are as reported and some are flagged as uncertain in that article.
factCheck.reference: MyJoyOnline, “Accra under water again: inside Ghana’s 66-year flooding crisis that nobody has fixed”.

pronunciation.guidance: Ghanaians often say "uh-KRAH" (stress on the second syllable).
